units.translation: O visible apparition of night, of dreams.
and in the night evils arose, storm-tossed.
the dark chariot of night hastens.
he brings night and darkness before the eyes.
when the sun departs into night, night loves to bring forth birth-pangs for a wise helmsman.
having fled to the sacred milking-time of black-maned night.
and these things I say to have seen in the night.
O Zeus, king, and friendly Night.
ancient children of Night. Thus Valckenarius for γραῖαι παλαιαὶ παῖδες [old women, ancient children].
grievous children of Night. Thus from the copies for αἰανῆς [grievous], about which I have spoken under the word αἰανής.
unfortunate maidens of Night, dishonored and mourning.

having shorn the nocturnal plain and the ill-fated shore, where it is said improperly for 'deadly' or 'unlucky', as Schuetz explained following the scholiast, 'having shorn the hateful plain along the ill-fated shore, that is, along Salamis', which interpretation is confirmed by the other word ἀκτάν [shore].
and the innermost Propontis, and likewise in Euripides Med. 211, where δι᾽ ἅλα νύχιον [through the nocturnal sea] is read, he wanted μύχιον [innermost] to be corrected.
the first nocturnal messenger of fire.

and nocturnal Hermes to watch over these sword-destroying contests. Where Hermann noted that νύχιον [nocturnal] is the same as χθόνιον [of the underworld], comparing Soph. OC 1559 ἐννυχίων ἄναξ, Αἰδωνεῦ Αἰδωνεῦ [lord of the night, Hades, Hades], and Trach. 501 τὸν ἔννυχον Ἅιδαν [the nocturnal Hades]. Therefore Hermann rightly wrote νύχιόν θ᾽ Ἑρμῆν [and nocturnal Hermes] for χθόνιον δ᾽ ἑρμῆα [and chthonic Hermes] (Ἑρμῆν [Hermes] Turnebus) and καὶ τὸν νύχιον [and the nocturnal one], which is in the gloss of M.
so that he may learn, being a sophist, that he is slower than Zeus.
wielding the helm of the city in the stern.
on the bronze-wrought shield he wielded the Sphinx, the eater of raw flesh, fastened with bolts.
moving a bright eyebrow in the darkness.
Justice – and she directs everything to its end, which is said by tmesis for ἐπινωμᾷ [directs upon].

about Tiresias observing the flight of birds and turning them over in his mind, 'wielding in his ears and mind, without fire, the oracular birds with unerring skill.' Where the scholiast says: 'For by hearing he distinguished the flights, not seeing, Tiresias.'
they have gone, alas, nameless, where νώνυμοι [nameless] is restored from the copies for νώνυμνοι [nameless].
so as to cross the sea on one's back.
and it falls not safely even on its back.
about Atlas, 'he groans, bearing the heavenly vault on his shoulders.' Thus I corrected for νώτοις ὑποστενάζει [groans under on his shoulders].
